name: Bisoctrizole
lead: Bisoctrizole (INCI: methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol, MBBT; trade names Tinosorb M, Parsol Max) is a phenolic bis-benzotriazole UV absorber used in sunscreens. It is made as microfine particles, usually supplied as a roughly 50% aqueous suspension, and is described as a hybrid between organic and particulate filters.[1][2]
It covers UVB and UVA and is reported to show little photodegradation. It is approved in the EU and other regions but has not been approved by the US FDA as a sunscreen active.[1][2]

Research is mostly formulation, skin-penetration and environmental work. One small registered trial examined it alongside titanium dioxide in solar urticaria; no study has examined it as an appearance treatment.

paras: Bisoctrizole dissolves poorly in both oil and water, so it is typically formulated as a particle suspension in the water phase, stabilised by a surfactant such as decyl glucoside.[2] Wikipedia says it is reported to help stabilise other filters, especially octinoxate, while flagging these claims as needing better citation.[2] A US drug label shows it combined with ethylhexyl triazone, diethylhexyl butamido triazone and DHHB in one product.[3]
Grokipedia adds that it is also used in some maxillofacial silicone prosthetics to resist UV degradation.[1]

A comparison of UVA protection from sunscreens containing butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane, MBBT or microfine zinc oxide used in vivo and in vitro methods.[4] In vitro percutaneous absorption work compared an organic and a mineral sunscreen and measured distribution in the stratum corneum.[5] Sprayable emulsions with high filter concentrations have also been tested for skin penetration in vitro.[6]

Wikipedia notes primary research reporting minimal skin penetration and no estrogenic effect in an in vitro assay or a rat uterotrophic test.[2] Grokipedia reports low acute toxicity and no evidence of irritation in standard tests.[1]

Bisoctrizole has been measured in European North and Baltic Sea sediment in a hazard assessment,[7] tested on brine shrimp and microalgae,[8] and included in an eco-compatibility assessment of newer-generation sunscreens.[9]
It is permitted in the EU (Grokipedia cites up to 10%) and in Canada, Australia and Japan; it has not been approved by the US FDA.[1][2]

A registered Phase 2 trial (n=16, 2007) evaluated microfine titanium dioxide, pigmentary titanium dioxide and bisoctrizole, alone and in combination, in people with idiopathic solar urticaria.[10] No other human trials specific to bisoctrizole were found; the in vivo UVA assessment of MBBT formulations is the other human-measured dataset.[4]

card.summary: A particle-form UV filter (Tinosorb M) that covers UVA and UVB; common abroad, not US-approved.
card.note: Not an FDA-approved sunscreen active; Wikipedia flags some property claims as weakly sourced.

quick.overview:
Bisoctrizole is a sunscreen ingredient sold as microfine particles. It absorbs UVA and UVB and is sometimes described as a hybrid between chemical and mineral filters.

It is approved in the EU and several other regions, but not by the US FDA.
quick.mechanism: The particles absorb UV and dissipate it as heat. It is often used alongside other filters.
quick.risks: Sources describe minimal skin penetration and no estrogenic activity in lab tests. Environmental studies have measured it in sediment and tested aquatic species.
